  "text": "The laundrette had one chair that nobody used because its front leg was shorter than the others.

Each morning, Ruth folded a piece of cardboard and pushed it underneath. Each evening, the cleaner threw it away.

A boy began coming on Saturdays with a blue laundry bag almost as tall as he was. He read the instructions on every machine before choosing the same one.

“Forty degrees,” Ruth told him. “Unless there’s wool.”

“There isn’t.”

He checked anyway.

While his clothes turned, he sat in the uneven chair with both feet planted on the floor.

“You can move,” Ruth said.

“I’m all right.”

The third week, he brought a small wooden wedge.

“My grandad made it.”

It fitted beneath the chair leg. Ruth nudged the seat, then sat down herself.

“Tell him thank you.”

“He said cardboard draws damp.”

She left a note for the cleaner.

In March, the boy came with a woman who counted coins into his hand. He showed her which compartment took the powder.

“Not that one,” he said. “That’s for later.”

Ruth stayed behind the counter.

Afterwards, the woman went outside to answer her phone.

“Mum’s home now,” the boy said.

“That’s nice.”

“She puts everything on sixty.”

They watched a red sleeve pass the glass.

He didn’t come the next Saturday. Someone left a newspaper on the chair, and by closing time three people had read it.

When Ruth lifted it away, she noticed the wedge had been painted blue.

She bent down to straighten it, although the chair no longer rocked."
